--account-id
(string)
Specifies the 12-digit account ID number of the Amazon Web Services account that you want to access or modify with this operation. If you don’t specify this parameter, it defaults to the Amazon Web Services account of the identity used to call the operation. To use this parameter, the caller must be an identity in the organization’s management account or a delegated administrator account. The specified account ID must be a member account in the same organization. The organization must have all features enabled , and the organization must have trusted access enabled for the Account Management service, and optionally a delegated admin account assigned.
Note
The management account can’t specify its ownAccountId
. It must call the operation in standalone context by not including theAccountId
parameter.To call this operation on an account that is not a member of an organization, don’t specify this parameter. Instead, call the operation using an identity belonging to the account whose contacts you wish to retrieve or modify.
Constraints:
- pattern:
^\d{12}$
--region-name
(string) [required]
Specifies the Region-code for a given Region name (for example,
af-south-1
). When you enable a Region, Amazon Web Services performs actions to prepare your account in that Region, such as distributing your IAM resources to the Region. This process takes a few minutes for most accounts, but it can take several hours. You cannot use the Region until this process is complete. Furthermore, you cannot disable the Region until the enabling process is fully completed.Constraints:
- min:
1
- max:
50

Deploy Universal Connectors on multiple PSM servers
This topic describes how to deploy a new PSM universal connector on all your PSM servers.
You can also run the Import connection component Rest API.
-
Prerequisite: Install the connection client
Install the connection client that you want to integrate on each of the PSM servers that should share this universal connector.
-
[Optional] Deploy the universal connector for testing.
Use this method to test the connector before distributing it to all the PSMs.
-
Copy the package to PSM\Packages folder.
-
Run the Deploy-Connectors.ps1, located under PSM\Scripts.
CD “C:\Program Files (x86)\CyberArk\PSM\Scripts” ./Deploy-Connectors.ps1
For troubleshooting, see the log under PSM\Logs\Scripts or run the script with the -Verbose option to display additional log messages.
After you have tested the connection component, you are ready to share it in the environment.
If a package does not exist in the PSMUniversalConnectors safe during the next configuration refresh, it is deleted from the PSM server.
-
-
Deploy universal connector on all PSM servers
Use this method to automatically deploy a new or updated PSM universal connectors on all of your PSM servers. A centralized repository simplifies management of PSM connectors in the environment and ensures that all servers are aligned with the identical connectors.
-
To deploy the universal connector to all the PSM servers in your environment, upload the package to the PSMUniversalConnectors Safe.
If you want to first test the connection component, see [Optional] Deploy the universal connector for testing..
-
All universal connectors in the PSMUniversalConnectors safe are deployed during the next configuration refresh in each PSM. The default configuration refresh interval is ten minutes.
If the connector package in the safe has been updated, it is also deployed to the PSM . If a connector package is deleted from the safe, it is removed from the PSM.
-
- For custom universal connectors, continue with Configure a Custom Universal Connector.
By default, all connectors added to the PSMUniversalConnectors Safe are automatically deployed to all PSM servers during the next configuration refresh of the PSM server.
To disable automatic connector deployment on a specific PSM, add the EnableConnectorsDeployment parameter to the PSM\basic_psm.ini of the PSM server and set the parameter value to "No".
-
Contact CyberArk Support and request that they delete the connector package from the PSMUniversalConnector Safe to remove it from the universal connector deployment.
-
In the PSM machine, delete connector files.
-
In the PSM machine > PSM\Hardening open the PSMConfigureAppLocker.xml file and remove any unnecessary rules from the AppLocker manually using one of the following options:
Option 1: Run the PSMConfigureAppLocker.ps1 ScriptRun the PSMConfigureAppLocker.ps1 script located under PSM/Hardening to reset the AppLocker and create rules based on the AppLockerConfiguration.xml file.
This script updates the AppLocker by deleting all existing rules and inserting the updated rules based on the PSM\Components\Connectors folder
Option 2: Remove each executable from the AppLocker manually-
Open the Local Security Policy
-
Go to Security Settings > Application Control Policies > AppLocker > Executable Rules
-
Locate the deny rule for PSMShadowUsers
-
Open the rule's properties.
-
Select the Exceptions tab. From the Exceptions lists, select the application you want to remove and click Remove
-
Press Apply and OK
-

Best practices for connector installation
Each SIA connector must be installed on a customer-side machine, so it can enable secure communication between your users and your organizational assets. This section provides CyberArk's recommendations for best practices about installing connectors.
-
Where to install SIA connectors
You can install an SIA connector on an existing machine, though we recommend using a dedicated machine as the connector host. Each connector should reside on a separate machine.
-
Time on connector host machines
Ensure the time on every connector host machine is set correctly. The time zone is irrelevant, but the machine's time should be synchronized with an internet time server.
-
Location of connector host machines
To reduce the latency of the connection, we recommend that connector host machines be geographically as close as possible to their targets. For example, the same region, zone, country, or city. You should also take into account network latency.
-
Assign connectors and define target sets
Each connector must be assigned to a connector pool either implicitly or explicitly. The target set is defined in the connector pool. By assigning a connector to a pool, you can define the connector's target set.
-
Number of connectors in a pool
For load balancing and high availability, install at least two connectors in each connector pool. Add more connectors to the pool on demand.
Connections to the target are established using three parallel connectors. The connection that opens first is used. For SSH and RDP connections, five parallel connectors are used to improve performance.
If multiple pools match the target address, the system opens at least one connection from each pool - up to the configured number of parallel connectors.
To support fallback to a connector that is located in a different geographical region, we recommend defining a pool for each data center with the same network coverage in each one.
-
Connecting to Windows targets
To support the provisioning process when connecting to Windows targets utilizing zero standing privileges or a vaulted credential and elevated permission, make sure you install the SIA connector on a Windows machine. The SIA connector can handle the provisioning only if it is installed on Windows.
-
Outbound access
The connector’s host machine must be configured to allow outbound access. For more information, see SIA network traffic requirements.
-
Follow your organization's standards and industry best practices for hardening protocols for target machines. For example, close any port or connection available to the connector machine, other than the ones required under SIA network traffic requirements.
-
Windows machines hosting connectors
Follow our recommendations about setting up Windows on machines hosting connectors. For more information, see Before you begin.
-
How to manage a SIA connector as a host
You can access a connector host by treating it as you would treat any other target. But we recommend that you have another SIA connector on a separate machine to ensure access to the connector host if the connector on the host fails.

System requirements
This topic describes the following system requirements for connector host machines.
-
Connectors must be installed on host machines in your network or domain to enable secure, isolated connections to platform resources when users sign in.
-
Connectors can be hosted on Windows or Linux machines. Linux machines generally perform more efficiently and are preferred, but not required. To connect to Windows machines via ZSP, at least one of the connectors in the pool must be installed on Windows to handle the provisioning.
-
Host machines must meet minimum specifications, as described in Server requirements.
CyberArk may choose not to provide maintenance and support services for CyberArk's Secure Infrastructure Access with relation to any of the platforms, systems, or targets that have reached their formal End-of-Life date, as published by their respective vendors from time to time. For more details, contact your CyberArk Support representative.

For information about Connector Management prerequisites for your connector machine operating system, drive settings, and user permissions, see Connector Management requirements.

For the best practices to follow when installing connectors, see Best practices for connector installation.

Manage discovery processes
This topic describes how to set up, view, and manage discovery processes.
Overview
To manage discovery processes, you must be a member of one of the following groups:
-
Vault admins
-
PVWAAccountsFeedAdmins
The Discovery process scans predefined machines for new and modified accounts and their dependencies. After the scan, you can see which accounts should be onboarded into the Vault where they can be managed automatically and securely, according to your enterprise compliance policies.
In the Discovery Management page, you can perform the following actions:
-
Create new discovery processes and view their statuses
-
View details of an existing discovery process in the Preview pane
-
Refresh the Discovery list to get a real-time update of the status of the discovery processes that are currently running in the system
The following information appears in the Discovery Setup area.

|---|---|
|
Discovery name |
The name of the defined discovery. |
|

The type of discovery process. Possible values:
|

|
|

The time on the scanner machine when this discovery starts. If this is a recurring discovery, this time indicates the last time this discovery was started. |
|

The status of the discovery the last time it was run. |

Create discovery processes
Before creating discovery processes, make sure that the user who performs the discovery has the required permissions, as listed in Accounts Feed supported target machines.
In organizations where privileged access is not permitted to remote Unix machines, a logon account that only has permission to log on remotely is required to log on to the remote machine. After this log on account has authenticated to the remote machine, the privileged user can run discoveries.
In these environments, before creating discoveries, associate a logon account to the account that will be used to run discoveries on remote Unix machines. For more information about creating and associating logon accounts, see Create linked accounts.
-
Log on to the PVWA with a user who is a member of the Vault Admins group.
-
In the ACCOUNTS page, under Accounts Management, click Accounts Discovery; the Pending Accounts page.
-
In the Pending Accounts page, click Discovery Management; the Discovery Management page appears.
-
In the Discovery Management page, click New Windows Discovery; the New Windows Accounts Discovery window appears.
-
Under Which account to use for scanning?, do the following:
-
Specify the Active Directory domain from which the list of machines to scan will be retrieved.
- Make sure that the PVWA machine has access to the Active Directory in order to show the tree-view of the OUs.
- Make sure that the CPM scanner that will perform the scan has access to the Active Directory.
- Specify the domain name in fully-qualified domain name (FQDN) format and with up to 170 characters.
-
To configure the discovery to connect to remote machines using an LDAPS secure connection, select Connect to the Active Directory using a secure connection.
-
By default, this option is selected.
-
Select the user who will perform the scan. Either select an account from the Vault or manually specify a user and password:
-
Select from Vault – Select a Vault account to run the scan. This is recommended for recurrent scans.
Make sure that the CPM selected for the scan has access to the Safe to which the account belongs.
-
Click Click to select an account from the Vault; a list of Vault accounts appears. These are all domain accounts in the specified domain.
-
Select the account to use for the discovery process, then click Select Account; details of the selected account are displayed.
Make sure the user in this account has the relevant permissions. For more information, refer to Manage discovery processes.
-
-
Specify Account – Specify a domain account that will run the scan.
-
User – The Active Directory user that will access the domain to retrieve the list of machines and will access each machine to perform the scan.
Specify the user name in a username or User Principal Name (UPN) format. Example: username@domain.com.
This user requires read permissions in the OU and all sub-OUs to scan.
Password – The domain user’s password.
-
-
-
Under What to scan?, specify the OU that will be scanned for accounts and their dependencies. You can either select it from the tree view or type its distinguished name.
-
To select the OU from a tree – Click Browse; the PVWA connects to the Active Directory using the user credentials specified in the 'Which user to use for scanning?' section and displays the accessible Active Directory tree.
-
If Connect to the Active Directory using a secure connection is selected, the PVWA connects to the Active Directory using a secure connection.
-
Select the OU to scan, then click OK; the selected OU appears in the Accounts Discovery window. This OU will be scanned recursively.
You can only select one OU. If no OUs are selected, by default, the selected domain will be scanned.
-
- To type the OU’s distinguished name – In OU to scan, type the distinguished name of the OU.
-
-
Under Which CPM scanner to use? select the CPM scanner that will scan for accounts and their dependencies. The CPM scanner will scan only machines that it can physically access.
-
If multiple CPM scanners are installed, select the relevant scanner from the drop-down list.
-
If only one CPM scanner is installed, only the name of that scanner will be displayed and it will be automatically selected.
-

-
Recurring – Enables you to define an automatic recurring discoveries. Specify the following details:
-
One time – Defines a one time discovery process that will run after you finish setting it up.
-

Accounts Feed
This section describes the Accounts Feed and how to configure and manage account discovery.
To perform Accounts Feed tasks, you must be a member of one of the following groups:
-
Vault admins
-
PVWAAccountsFeedAdmins
CyberArk’s Accounts Feed introduces the next generation workflow of discovering and provisioning privileged accounts. This workflow is aligned with business processes in order to simplify and accelerate the deployment and management of privileged account security. The Accounts Feed process is divided into three main steps:
| ■ | Discover – Automated privileged account discovery, which is designed to quickly locate critical accounts and credentials. |
| ■ | Analyze – A view of all discovered accounts, which enables you to analyze and determine the accounts that are no longer needed, and delete them, and assess the risk of each account. |
| ■ | Provision – The scope of the accounts to manage can be provisioned in the Vault in a simple and intuitive way. |
The Privileged Access Manager - Self-Hosted solution scans your machines according to the source that was defined such as Active Directory or a CSV file, to discover privileged accounts in your organization (such as Windows and Unix accounts) and their dependencies (such as Windows Services). This gives you a clear and comprehensive picture of existing accounts in your organization.
PAM - Self-Hosted uses the CyberArk Central Policy Manager Scanner to run account discoveries. A scanner is installed with each CPM in your environment, enabling you to scan all distributed networks in your organization.
When scanning a specified domain, the CPM Scanner automatically retrieves information about discovered accounts that are stored in trusted domains, without requiring additional permission. Likewise, the CPM Scanner can retrieve information about discovered accounts from trusted domains in the forest trust. This is only available for direct trusts.
However, in order to discover accounts (not just information about them) in domains that are not specified as the source, the user who runs the discovery requires permissions in those domains.
All the detected accounts are displayed in the Pending Accounts page in the PVWA, where you can view them and onboard them, based on various criteria that you can define. You can schedule account discoveries to run automatically, once or at regular intervals, streamlining account management and ensuring that the pending account list contains the most up-to-date details about the privileged accounts in your environment. Then you can view recurring discoveries and see when they last ran, when they’ll next run, and how long each one took.

Configure audit and monitor log files
This topic describes how to configure the location and behavior of the log files.
By default, the Credential Provider displays a generic message when a warning or error occurs. Full details of the issue are available in the APPConsole.log file, which is restricted.
To enable verbose error logs, you can update the VerboseErrors parameter, although this is not recommended. For more information, see Configure debug levels.
Log file location
The following parameter in the basic configuration file specifies the location of the Credential Provider log files:
| LogsFolder | The full pathname of the folder where the Credential Provider stores the local logs file. |
Configure debug levels
The following parameters in the main configuration file specify the level of debugging in the log files:
| Parameter | Description |
|---|---|
| AppProviderDebugLevels |
Sets the debug level of the Credential Provider. You can set several values, separated by commas. 0 - No messages are written to the trace log (default). 1 - Credential Provider errors are written to the trace log . 2 - Credential Provider trace messages are written to the trace log . 3 - Credential Provider CASOS errors are written to the trace log. 4 - Credential Provider CASOS activities and trace messages are written to the trace log. 5 - Credential Provider background refresh trace messages are written to the trace log. |
| ProtocolDebugLevels |
Sets the debug level of the protocol layer. You can set several values, separated by commas. 0 - No messages are written to the trace log (default). 1 - Protocol errors are written to the trace log. 2 - Protocol trace messages are written to the trace log. |
| CacheDebugLevels |
Sets the debug level of the Credential Provider cache. You can set several values, separated by commas. 0 - No messages are written to the trace log (default). 1 - Cache errors are written to the trace log. 2 - Cache trace messages are written to the trace log. |
| AuthenticationLogs |
Whether or not the log provides indications for two authentications. For more information, see Security best practices. Yes - Log provides indications about two authentications (default). No - Log does not provide indications about two authentications. |
| VerboseErrors |
Whether or not error details are provided in the Windows Event Viewer or syslog. Yes - Logs and responses include error details. No - Logs and responses are replaced with a generic message. Detailed logs and responses appear only in APPConsole.log (default). For zOS 12.6, this value must be set to Yes. |
Archive logs in the Vault
The following parameters in the main configuration file specify when the log file is archived on the local machine:
| LogRetentionOnSizeMB |
The size (in MB) of the log files when they are moved to a subfolder of the Log folder. New log files are started automatically. The default value is 25 MB.
|
| LogRetentionOnTimeIntervalMinutes |
The number of minutes after which the log files are moved to a subfolder of the Logs folder. New log files are started automatically.
|
Delete old logs
The following parameters in the main configuration file specify when old log files are deleted:
| OldLogsRetention |
The number of days that trace and console log files stored in the ‘Old’ subfolder of the Logs folder are saved, after which they are deleted. By default, log files are saved for 30 days. The Credential Provider automatically searches every hour for log files to delete; this cannot be configured. To prevent old log files from being deleted, specify 0 (zero). If this parameter is changed from zero to a positive number or vice versa, the change is only applied after the Credential Provider is restarted. |
| OldAuditLogsRetention |
The number of days that audit log files stored in the ‘Old’ subfolder of the Logs folder are saved, after which they are deleted. By default, old audit log files are saved for 90 days. The Credential Provider automatically searches for log files to delete every hour; this cannot be configured. To prevent old log files from being deleted, specify 0 (zero). If this parameter is changed from zero to a positive number or vice versa, the change is only applied after the Credential Provider is restarted. |

Caching
This topic describes caching in the Credential Provider.
To reduce the load on the Vault, always configure a caching mechanism.
Overview
The Credential Provider can use a local cache to store information that is supplied to users even when there is a network failure and the Vault cannot be accessed. Information in the cache is encrypted and can only be accessed with the same authentication criteria that are required to retrieve information from the Vault, while constantly tracking and monitoring all user activities. This facilitates uninterrupted workflows, increasing productivity, and providing a focused and seamless business environment.
The cache contains the following information:
|
Passwords |
This information includes passwords and their properties. |
|
Application List |
This information includes application properties and details and is used to authenticate applications. |
|
Applications/Password table |
This information includes details about the connection between applications and passwords. It is used for access control and ensures that applications can only access the passwords that they require. |
All the information in the cache is refreshed and synchronized with the Vault at periodic intervals. Any changes in passwords or Vault configuration are reflected in the cache after a refresh process, either automatically according to the CacheRefreshInterval parameter in the main configuration file, or by forcing a refresh process using the appprvmgr utility. For more information about this utility, see Credential Provider utility.
The Credential Provider supports three levels of caching. The caching level is specified in the central configuration file in the CacheLevel parameter.
|
Level |
Description |
|---|---|
|
None |
The Credential Provider does not cache any password information and accesses the Vault directly for each password request that it receives. |
|
Memory |
The Credential Provider caches password information in local memory. The Credential Provider does not access the Vault for each password request, but rebuilds the cache each time that it restarts. |
|
Persistent |
The Credential Provider caches all the information that it needs to operate in a local secure storage as well as in memory. The name of the cache file is specified in the CacheFile parameter. This makes the Credential Provider completely independent of network performance and the Vault, and ensures constant access to passwords. This level has two modes that specify where to store the cache file encryption key. For information about these modes, see Persistent cache level. |
How does it work?
The Credential Provider maintains a cache that stores password content and properties, and authentication and accessibility details, and constantly updates the cache according to the parameters set in the configuration files. The Credential Provider accesses the Vault regularly to retrieve updated password content and to refresh the cache so that the application receives accurate passwords.
The Credential Provider accesses the Vault to retrieve passwords in the following scenarios:
-
The password, application details, or application/password connection information are not stored in the cache. After installing the Credential Provider and configuring it, a password is retrieved to the cache the first time that an application requests it.
-
The password in the cache is marked with an indication of an upcoming password change process.
-
The Credential Provider is configured to not use the cache.
-
During a background cache refresh process.
During password requests, as well as in the background refresh, when the Credential Provider needs to access the Vault to retrieve the password (based on the above scenarios), it uses the Credential Provider user and checks that the application is defined in the Vault and has the relevant access permissions to the requested passwords.
Following a password request, if the Credential Provider accessed the Vault (using the Credential Provider user), the following cache modifications may occur:
-
Add the application, password, or application/password connection to the cache if they exist in the Vault
-
Update password content and properties, and application properties
During password requests, the Credential Provider does not remove existing passwords from the cache; passwords are only removed from the cache during a background cache refresh process. This means that if you have changed an application user’s permissions to prevent it from retrieving a password, the password remains in the cache where the application can still retrieve it until the next background cache refresh process, after which the application is not able to retrieve it.
Background cache refresh process
A background process refreshes the cache with the information that the Credential Provider has retrieved from the Vault at regular intervals, according to the CacheRefreshInterval parameter in the main configuration file. As the background refresh process uses the Credential Provider user to access the Vault, the Credential Provider user must have permissions in the Safes where the application credential resides in the Vault. For more information about building the Vault environment for applications, refer to Build the environment for the Credential Provider.
The background process manages the following tasks:
-
Updating the password, application details, and application/password connection information in the cache and synchronizing it with updated details in the Vault. The background refresh process never adds new passwords to the cache.
-
Verifying cache integrity to ensure that all the information is accurate and up-to-date.
-
Removing any information from the cache in any of the following scenarios:
-
Information has been deleted from the Vault.
-
The application user or the Credential Provider user is no longer authorized to access information that is stored in the cache. (The user does not have the required Safe authorizations to access passwords.)
-
A password hasn't been requested for a certain amount of time - configurable by the TTL configuration.
-
The following image shows how the Credential Provider retrieves information from the Vault and stores it in the cache, which is constantly updated by the background process. Whenever an application requests a password, it receives the most recent one.
The cache is refreshed periodically from the Vault, depending on the following parameters in the central configuration file:
|
Parameter |
Description |
|---|---|
|
CacheRefreshInterval |
How frequently (in seconds) the applications cache is refreshed from the Vault. |
|
AutomaticParmsRefreshInterval |
How frequently (in seconds) the main configuration file on the Credential Provider machine is refreshed from the Vault. This parameter refreshes the configuration file specified in the AppProviderVaultParmsFile parameter, as well as the Credential Provider-specific configuration file if it exists. |
If the Vault is inaccessible due to network issues, the Credential Provider calculates a period of time during which it avoids accessing the Vault. The length of this period is calculated according to the number of Credential Providers installed in the Vault – the more Credential Providers installed on the Vault, the longer the Credential Provider may take to reconnect to the Vault. During this time the Credential Provider serves all requests from its local cache.
If the Vault is inaccessible due to an authentication error that requires manual intervention, for example if the Credential Provider user is suspended, the Credential Provider stops trying to connect to the Vault until it is restarted. During this time, the Credential Provider serves all requests from its local cache. This scenario is very rare and should never happen in a live environment.
These parameters can only be modified in the central configuration file in the Vault.
Implement the local cache
Whenever the Credential Provider receives a password request, it refers to the local cache for the password instead of accessing the Vault directly. This provides applications with constant access, regardless of network performance and Vault accessibility. The background process described above accesses the Vault regularly to refresh the local cache so that the Credential Provider always provides accurate passwords.
Persistent cache level
Persistent cache level modes specify where the cache file encryption key is stored. These modes provide different security levels and network performance dependencies.
The modes are enabled using the KeyStorage parameter that is configured in the Credential Provider configuration file. For more information, see Credential Provider configuration files.
|
Mode |
Description |
||
|---|---|---|---|
|
Local |
Makes the Credential Provider completely independent of network performance and the Vault, and ensures constant access to passwords. This mode provides limited security because the cache file encryption key is stored locally on the Credential Provider machine. |
||
|
Vault |
The Credential Provider cache file encryption key is stored in the Vault in a dedicated Safe named AppProviderCacheSafe. This Safe is created as part of the installation process. If the KeyStorage parameter is set to Vault, the Credential Provider creates a new account named <Credential_Provider_user_name>_key on this Safe. By default, the Credential Provider user name in the Vault is Prov_<Hostname>. Every time that the Credential Provider starts, it retrieves the cache file encryption key from the cache Safe.
If you change the KeyStorage value from Local to Vault, the Credential Provider creates its key in AppProviderCacheSafe and the cache must be decrypted and encrypted with this key. The cache does not have to be rebuilt in this case. |
|
When the Credential Provider loads, if it encounters a corrupted cache file, it creates a backup version of the corrupted cache file in the same folder and creates a new cache file. |

This topic describes how to set up the Credential Provider environment.
|
For optimal performance guidelines, see Recommendations for best performance and limitations. |
Overview
You can configure the Credential Provider to create a flexible identity management system that answers your specific needs.
The Credential Provider configuration parameters are stored in two configuration files, both of which are accessed with the Credential Provider user.
|
Configuration file |
Description |
|---|---|
| basic_appprovider.conf |
This is the Credential Provider's local configuration file. It specifies the location of the central configuration file in the Vault, and the parameters that are required to log onto the Vault and retrieve the main configuration file. |
|
This is the main configuration file. It contains all the parameters that determine how the Credential Provider works. During installation, this file is copied to the Credential Provider Safe (by default, is called AppProviderConf) in the Vault. This file can serve as a central configuration file for multiple Credential Providers running on the same type of operating system. If a Credential Provider requires different parameter values to those defined in the central configuration file, you can specify its own main configuration file. For details, see: |
Shared configuration
Several Credential Providers running on the same type of operating system can access the same main configuration file to determine how they work. In this setup, we refer to the main configuration file as the central configuration file.
To configure a shared configuration for multiple Credential Providers, you need to make sure that each Credential Provider's local configuration file (basic_appprovider.conf) specifies the same Vault, the same configuration Safe, and the same main configuration file.
To set up a shared configuration:
-
Install the first Credential Provider. See the relevant instructions for your implementation platform in Install the Credential Provider.
Note the values that you use for the Configuration Safe name and the main configuration file name. You will use these values again in the next step.
-
For each of the other Credential Providers, install the Credential Provider using the instructions relevant to its implementation platform. During installation, specify the same Configuration Safe name and main configuration file name as you specified when you installed the first Credential Provider in the previous step.
The installation does not overwrite the main configuration file that was created when you installed the first Credential Provider.
-
In the Vault, make sure that the Credential Provider user has the following authorizations on the Safe that contains the central configuration file:
- List Files
- Retrieve Files
- Create Files
- Update Files
- Update File Properties
- Rename Files
- View Audit
- View Owners
- Use Password
- Initiate Password Management Operations
- Initiate CPM Change with Manual Password
- Create/Rename Folder
- Move Files/Folders
Credential Provider-specific configuration
In a multi-Credential Provider environment, you can create a customized main configuration file for a specific Credential Provider. This Credential Provider uses its customized main configuration file rather than the central configuration file used by all the other Credential Providers (see Shared configuration above).
|
Any parameter defined in a Credential Provider-specific configuration file must be declared in the main configuration file; parameters that are not declared in the main configuration file are discarded. Declare each parameter in the main configuration with its default value and then set the relevant value in the Credential Provider-specific configuration for each provider. |
The Credential Provider-specific configuration file's name reflects the name of the Credential Provider that it applies to, and is stored in the same Safe and folder as the central configuration file.
To create a customized main configuration file:
-
Make a copy of the central configuration file in the same Safe (by default AppProviderConf), and rename the copied file using the following naming convention:
main_appprovider.conf.<platform>.<version>.<Provider’s Vault username>
Alternatively you can use a copy of the sample main configuration file which is copied to the Env folder during installation.
The copied file must use the same naming convention described above, and must be stored in the same Vault as the central configuration file.

Open the copied file and customize the parameter values for the specific Credential Provider. For details, see Credential Provider (CP) configuration files. Make sure to specify the section title for the parameters.

The Windows environment on the Credential Provider machine
By default, the Credential Provider installation folders are created under C:\Program Files\CyberArk.
The ApplicationPasswordProvider folder
This folder contains all subfolders that are created for this environment. In addition, it contains the executable files that are needed and the local configuration file. These subfolders and files are detailed below:
| Subfolder/File | Description |
|---|---|
| Cache | Contains the protected storage file that the Credential Provider uses as its cache. It is created automatically the first time that the Credential Provider retrieves passwords from the Vault. By default, the cache is called appprovider_cache.db, although its name can be changed in the main configuration file. |
| Env |
Contains the utilities that are required to create the Credential Provider environment in the Digital Vault during installation. This folder also contains the Log subfolder where the log files created during installation are stored. In addition, this folder contains the default Credential Provider configuration file, main_appprovider.default.conf and the local copy of the shared configuration file, main_appprovider.conf.<platform>.<version>. |
| Logs | Contains the console, audit, and trace log files that track the Credential Provider activity and access to passwords in the cache. |
| Temp | Contains files that are used by the Credential Provider for internal processing. |
| Utils | Contains the utilities that are used to calculate the unique hash value of an application/script, and can be used to authenticate an application to the Credential Provider. |
| Vault |
Contains the Vault parameter file which specifies which Digital Vault will be accessed by the Credential Provider and the Credential Provider user credential file that will enable the Credential Provider to authenticate to the Vault. It also contains the utility that is used to create user credential files for application users to authenticate to the Digital Vault. For more information about creating user credential files, see Credential file usage in Credential Providers (CP). |
| AppProvider.exe | Used to run the Credential Provider. |
| AppPrvMgr.exe | The Credential Provider management utility. |
| Basic_appprovider.conf | The basic Credential Provider configuration file. |
The ApplicationPasswordSdk folder
This folder contains the SDK executables and libraries that are required to run the various Application Password SDKs. For more information, see Application Password SDKs.

Self-hosted products
This topic describes the end-of-life policy for CyberArk self-hosted products and lists the end-of-life dates.
Version numbering
Version numbering refers to a specific edition of a product indicated by the assigned version number, based on M.N.P format (e.g., v.12.5.1):
-
M - Major version number
-
N - Minor version number
-
P - Patch-set number
Release content
|
Type of release |
Description |
|---|---|
|
Major |
Typically includes major new features and/or significant software architectural changes. |
|
Minor |
Typically includes minor functionality modifications, enhancements and minor software architectural changes. |
|
Patch |
Typically includes bug fixes and minimal software adjustments to a Major or Minor version. Released on an as-needed basis. |
Definitions
The following table describes the definitions used in the EOL dates for self-hosted products.
|
Definition |
Description |
|---|---|
|
Support Period |
The period in which CyberArk customer support provides technical support with regards to a product version, including problem verification and determination, temporary fixes, if applicable, and fixes that were developed during the version’s Development Period. This does not include support that requires engineering efforts or development of new code fixes. |
|
End-of-Support Date |
The date on which the Support Period ceases. Support tickets submitted prior to the End of Support Date will not be affected. |
|
Development Period |
The period in which CyberArk provides code analysis and maintenance for a product version, including code fixes as necessary.
|
|
End-of-Development Date |
The date on which the Development Period ceases.
|
-
There may be circumstances in which - despite CyberArk’s reasonable commercial efforts - resolving an issue will require upgrading to a newer version, even if the version is still in its Development Period (for example if a fix requires significant architectural changes or includes substantial changes to third party software dependencies, which make delivering a patch to an older version not feasible).
-
Similarly, in the event underlying platforms, browsers, and/or systems incorporated in a CyberArk product, are no longer supported by their respective vendor, or are not properly maintained by their vendors, CyberArk may be required to shorten the Development Period of the version which relies on such systems in order to comply with appropriate security and performance levels of its products.
Version support levels
Each version is assigned with a specific support level – Standard Term Support (STS) or Long Term Support (LTS) – which defines the version’s scope and duration of technical support and code maintenance, as further detailed in this section.
Any version that is not specifically designated as LTS is considered STS.
Long Term Support (LTS)
-
During the Development Period, CyberArk backports high and critical severity security bug fixes, and critical severity functionality bug fixes. LTS versions offer a longer Development Period than STS versions, as indicated by the End of Development Dates in the EOL dates for self-hosted products.
-
The Support Period may be extended by the customer for the duration indicated in the EOL dates for self-hosted products, subject to payment of additional applicable fees. In any event, it is not possible to extend the Development Period.
-
Fixes for LTS versions of PAM - Self-Hosted products require that all components are on the same LTS version.
-
CyberArk only supports upgrades from one LTS version to another or to the latest version release. This is designed to avoid inadvertently downgrading security or stability fixes that are included in LTS patches or in the latest version release.
Standard Term Support (STS)
During the Development Period, CyberArk backports critical severity security bug fixes.
EOL dates for self-hosted products
The actual end date is the last day of the listed month.
The end-of-life dates apply to the original version as well as their patches.

CIS benchmark compatibility for Central Credential Provider
This topic describes the environment and tests that were done for CIS Benchmark compatibility with Central Credential Provider.
CIS Benchmark compatibility is only possible when using a dedicated machine for Central Credential Provider. It is not possible when Central Credential Provider is installed on the same machine as PVWA.
Overview
The Center for Internet Security (CIS) Benchmarks are a set of globally recognized and consensus-driven best practices to help security practitioners implement and manage their cybersecurity defenses.
The CIS Benchmarks are industry standard security and hardening guidelines and best practices.
By following step-by-step CIS Benchmark recommendations on your Central Credential Provider machine, you will follow the industry's standards for Central Credential Provider hardening.
For more information about the CIS Benchmark, see https://www.cisecurity.org/benchmark/microsoft_iis.
The following sections describe the process we followed in order to be compatible with the CIS Benchmark. We recommend that you follow these steps in your environment, as well as following hardening and security recommendations.
Testing environment
The following testing environment was used:
-
CIS Microsoft IIS 10 Benchmark v1.1.1 - 03-13-2019
-
Microsoft Windows Server 2016
-
CyberArk Central Credential Provider (including Credential Provider with the same version)
-
v12.6
-
v13.0
-
Test flow
-
Installed and configured Credential Provider and Central Credential Provider to run on a clean machine with version 12.6.
-
Implemented all changes manually as recommended in the 'CIS Microsoft IIS Benchmark' document.
-
Performed tests to verify that the Central Credential Provider is working properly.
-
Upgraded Credential Provider and Central Credential Provider to version 13.0.
-
Verified that the 'CIS Microsoft IIS Benchmark' recommendations are still implemented.
-
Performed tests again to verify that the Central Credential Provider v13.0 is working properly.

Discovery scan requirements
This topic describes the what you need before you can run account discovery scans.
Before you begin
-
Ensure that connector pools have been set up properly in your system:
-
Your organization networks are defined.
-
At least one connector pool is set up and includes the relevant end points and identifiers.
-
At least one Connector Management agent is defined.
-
Connector Management agents version v1.0.581 or later.
Learn about connector pools and networks and how to define them.
Make sure that Microsoft .NET Framework 4.8 is installed on the connector machine.
-
-
Ensure the system is configured for the ports used by the discovery service to access remote machines. See Ports used for account discovery.
The SaaS discovery solution is supported by port 636 for LDAPs connectivity.
-
Ensure that you are assigned to a relevant role.
-
Prepare a CSV file:
-
For Windows and *Nix scans that use a CSV file, set up a file that contains the list of machines you want to scan based on the predefined file format. Download the sample CSV file as described in the steps for defining a new file-based scan.
-
For database scans, set up a CSV file that contains the details of the databases that you want to scan. Download the sample CSV file as described in the steps for defining a new scan.
-
Database scan requirements
Before scanning databases, make sure make sure the relevant drivers and certificates are installed.
-
Secure SSL connections between the connector and database require certificates. Add a trusted certificate on both the target database and each connector that has access to scan the target database.
-
Make sure the required drivers are installed on the connector machines. See the drivers in the database parameters table below.
-
For each connector you plan to use for database scanning, open the required network paths on the connector machine to the database’s relevant ports. Each database has a default port, but you can specify an alternative in the CSV file.
Discovery supports driver installation in 64 bit only.
| Database |
Parameter |
|---|---|
|
SQL Server |
Default port: 1433 Default database: "master" Required driver: ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server (64 bit) |
|
Postgres SQL |
Default port: 5432 Default database: "postgres" Required driver: PostgreSQL ODBC Driver (UNICODE) 17.00.00.06 (64 bit) |

Configure scan certificate validation
Discovery scans support both certificate validation and non-validation modes. For secure environments, CyberArk recommends keeping certificate validation enabled whenever possible. Perform these steps on the connector machine that has access to the domain you plan to scan.
Disable certificate validation
For security reasons, we recommend keeping certificate validation enabled. However, if you trust the connector’s certificate and prefer to run the scan without certificate validation, there are two ways to do this:
-
When defining a scan (recommended): Under Certificate validation, disable the Validate installed certificate during scans setting. For more information, see Define discovery scans for databases.
-
Configure the connector machine’s Registry as described below.
Once this setting is applied, scans will run without validating server certificates.
-
Connect to the connector machine that has access to the target domain.
-
Press Win + R, type
regedit
, and press Enter to open the Registry Editor. -
Navigate to the following location: HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\SOFTWARE\CyberArk\DiscoveryConfig
If this path does not exist:
-
Right-click SOFTWARE, select New > Key, and name it CyberArk.
-
Under CyberArk, create another key named DiscoveryConfig.
-
In the DiscoveryConfig key, right-click in the right pane and select New > String Value.
-
Name the new value DisableCertValidation.
-
Double-click the new value and set its Value data to True.
If you disable certificate validation using the Registry, this will remain even if you enable the Validate installed certificate during scans setting in the UI. To reverse it, you will need to go back into the Registry and set DisableCertValidation to False. This is why we recommend performing this task in the UI rather than in the Registry.

Configure Applocker
This section describes how to configure the AppLocker policy by editing PSMConfigureAppLocker.xml file. Use this reference when you run the AppLocker script manually.
AppLocker rules
To create a hardened and secure PSM environment, the system must limit the applications that can be launched during a PSM session. To do this, the PSM uses the Windows AppLocker feature, which defines a set of rules that allow or deny applications from running on the PSM machine, based on unique file identities. These rules specify which users or groups can run those applications.
The PSM installation includes an AppLocker script which enables PSM users to invoke internal PSM applications, mandatory Windows applications, and third- party external applications that are used as clients in the PSM.
All AppLocker rules are defined in the PSMConfigureAppLocker.xml file in the PSM installation folder > Hardening.
-
If your environment includes executables that must be allowed, in addition to those that are built-in to the PSM installation, such as PSM Universal Connectors executables, you must edit this file to add rules that will allow these executables.
Any changes or additions you make to the default configurations of the AppLocker file may affect the security of your environment, and are outside of CyberArk’s control. It is your responsibility to verify these changes are in line with your organization's security policies.
-
If you have connectors deployed using shared universal connector deployment on multiple PSM servers they will be updated automatically in the AppLocker rules. For details, see Deploy Universal Connectors on multiple PSM servers. Associated executables are automatically updated in the AppLocker rules.
Configure and run the AppLocker script
-
Edit the PSMConfigureAppLocker.xml file, if necessary, so that all applications you need to run exist as <Application> tags under <AllowedApplications>.
-
To run the PSMConfigureAppLocker.ps1 script, open a PowerShell window and run the following command:
“<PSM installation folder>\Hardening\PSMConfigureAppLocker.ps1”
Detect blocked DLL files
Any changes or additions you make to the default configurations of the AppLocker file may affect the security of your environment and are beyond CyberArk’s control. It is your responsibility to verify these changes are in line with your organization's security policies.
If a connector fails, run the executable related to this connector and rerun the AppLocker script.
If the connector is still blocked, do the following:
-
Open the Windows Event viewer.
-
Go to Applications and Services Logs\Microsoft\Windows\Applocker\EXE and DLL.
-
In the left page, right-click EXE and DLL and select clear log…. Select Save and clear to back up the logged events.
-
Initiate a connection with the relevant connection through the PVWA.
-
Go back to Applications and Services Logs\Microsoft\Windows\Applocker\EXE and DLL.
-
in the left pane, right-click EXE and DLL and click refresh.
-
In the right pane, click Filter Current Log… and under Event Level only select Error and click OK.
-
Filter for Error 8004.
-
For each blocked dll error found, add a relevant line to the PSMConfigureAppLocker.xml under AllowedApplications in the dll section.
-
Convert the AppLocker path into an absolute path based on the Microsoft documentation.
For example, if the AppLocker path is %OSDRIVE%\ORACLE\INSTANTCLIENT\OCI.DLL, replace %OSDRIVE% with %SystemDrive%, a Windows environment variable. The new path will be %SystemDrive%\ORACLE\INSTANTCLIENT\OCI.DLL.
-
Open PowerShell, type in the following command, and press Enter:
[System.Environment]::ExpandEnvironmentVariables("<Converted Full Path Of DLL>")
-
Using the absolute path returned from the previous step (in our example, ORACLE\INSTANTCLIENT\OCI.DLL), add the new dll exception under AllowedApplications. The method should be Hash, but can also be Publisher or Path.
<Libraries Name="UniqueName" Type="Dll" Path="<DLL Absolute Full Path>" Method="Hash" />
-
To run the PSMConfigureAppLocker.ps1 script, open a PowerShell window and run the following command:
“<PSM installation folder>\Hardening\PSMConfigureAppLocker.ps1”
-
Repeat the process (steps 1-9) until the connector works properly.

Clean the Shadow user profile
This section describes how to configure PSM to clean Shadow user profiles.
When users initiate a connection (session) to a target machine via PSM, a PSM Shadow user is automatically created on the PSM machine and that's the user that is used to log on to the target machine and perform actions.
The purpose of the Shadow user is to isolate the session. This enables programs launched on the same server by different
During the established session, some information is saved in the Shadow user profile, which can ultimately fill up the PSM server's storage.
PSM includes an automatic cleanup process in order to manage the PSM server's storage space. You can change the default settings, such as the threshold of the Shadow user profile folder size or which subfolders to empty.
For the full list of settings, see Shadow user profile settings.
When the user profile folder exceeds the set threshold, the end user receives a warning at the beginning of the session.
To modify the default settings of the Shadow user profile:

Connect through Privileged Session Manager for Windows
This topic describes transparent connections to target systems using a standard RDP client application.
Connect to target systems directly from your desktop using any standard RDP client application to benefit from a native user experience.
Requirements
-
The PSM server must be hardened. For details, refer to PSM Hardening Tasks.
-
Connections can be made from Unix / Linux / Mac / Windows end user machines.
- To connect using a smart card:
- Smart card drivers must be installed on the PSM machine
- The smart card must include a valid certificate
- The Vault must be configured with LDAP integration
Considerations
Before using your standard RDP client application to connect through PSM to your target system, review the following considerations:
-
Settings for drives, printers and clipboard redirection specified in the connection component level are enforced, and platform level configurations are ignored.
If the End User connects through PSM without providing the target system details and selects a connection component (other than PSM-RDP) with those settings enforced, the user cannot connect using that connection component. The drives redirection setting is enforced only for the PSM-RDP connection component .
-
Connections that require additional information from the user when the connection is established (user parameters) cannot be initiated using an RDP client application.
-
Dual control is not supported. Instead, use the PVWA.
If your request to use the account is approved, you are able to connect to this account using an RDP client application.
-
One-time passwords are supported. For details, see Change passwords
- Connections made from an RDP client application are Remote Desktop connections, and not RemoteApp connections.
-
The username for connecting to a target cannot contain an at sign (@), which is reserved for domain users.
-
The built-in connection component for RDP connections via PSM is PSM-RDP.
-
Connections that require prompting for user parameters are not supported. To avoid prompting for user parameters, when connecting to Windows machines, ask your Vault administrator to set any user parameters, such as the LogonDomain, in the account details.
-
To connect to your target machine using a domain account, append the domain name to the username used to log in to the target machine.
-
The built-in connection component for SSH connections through PSM are PSM-SSH and PSM-Telnet.
-
To connect your target machine using a domain/NIS account, append the domain name to the username used to log in to the target machine.
-
The built-in connection components for databases connections via PSM are PSM-Toad, PSM-SQLPlus and PSM-SQLServerMgmtStudio.
-
Connections with Toad or SQLPlus connection components with the SYS user or any other privileged user that require selection of the role that will be used to connect to the remote database, cannot be initiated using an RDP client application. Use PVWA for such connections.
-
The built-in connection component for VMWare connections via PSM is PSM-VSPHERE.
- You can connect to VMWare machines through PSM in any of the following ways:
Connect to a VMWare ESX machine transparently - The user is automatically logged onto the remote ESX
Connect to a vCenter transparently using a Personal Account - The user is prompted for their user and password and is then logged onto the remote vCentre machine
Connect to a vCenter transparently using a Shared Account - The user is logged onto the remote vCenter machine with the shared account.

CACert utility
This topic describes the CACert utility.
Overview
The CACert utility prepares and manages the certificate that the Vault will use to create a secure channel to a client, so that users can authenticate to the third party securely. After the CACert utility has run, a log file is created which contains details about the process that was carried out.
See Certificate requirements for detailed requirements. |
The following procedures must be performed on each Vault server, according to its configuration.
|
The configuration described below shows the recommended settings for most use cases. See below for all the CACert options. |
Create the SSL certificate for the Vault server
There are two ways you can create an SSL certificate for the Vault server:
-
Generate a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to be signed by your organizational Certificate Authority (CA), and install the certificate on the Vault
-
Import a certificate for the Vault that was created externally
Generate and install the Vault certificate
First you must create a Certificate Signing Request (CSR) to be signed by your organization's SSL. Next you sign the CSR using your organization's Certificate Authority (CA). Last, you install the issued certificate on the Vault server.
Step 1: Generate a Certificate Signing Request for the Vault
This procedure creates a private key on the Vault server and a CSR to be signed by your organization's SSL.
- Navigate to the Vault server installation folder (by default: c:\Program Files (x86)\PrivateArk\Server).
- Open a Command window as an Administrator.
-
Run the following command to create a new Certificate Signing Request (CSR):
CACert.exe request
- Name of the request output file - The file name of the request for the Vault server.
-
Private key output file - The file name of the private key for the Vault server.
-
Enter a path that is different from the default path.
-
The path cannot contain any quote symbols (").
-
- Common Name - The Vault server common name.
-
Subject Alternative Names - List of Subject Alternative Names including the hostname and IP addresses. If the Vault is in a Cluster architecture, enter both the private and virtual IP address.
You can enter multiple alternative DNS and/or IP values in the Subject Alternative Names field. The format is <field name>:<alternative_name>,<field name>:<alternative_name>. For example, DNS:hostname,IP:10.10.10.10,IP:11.11.11.11
- Provide the CSR to your organization's Certificate Authority (CA).
Step 2: Sign the CSR using your organization's Certificate Authority (CA)
The signed certificate and the chain certificate must be in base-64 format.
Step 3: Install your Vault Server Organization SSL Certificate
This procedure installs your signed organizational SSL certificate in the Vault application.
- Transfer the Vault certificate to the Vault server.
- If you use Session Management in Distributed Vaults, transfer the Certificate Chain to the Vault server.
- Back up the current server private key. The path to the key can be found in the ServerPrivateKey parameter in DBParm.ini.
- Replace the existing server private key file with the new private key created above.
- Navigate to the Vault server installation folder (by default, c:\Program Files (x86)\PrivateArk\Server).
- Open a Command window as an administrator.
- Run the following command:
CACert.exe install
Specify the path to the Vault server certificate.
- Restart the Vault application.
Import your organization's SSL certificate for the Vault server
This procedure imports your organization's SSL certificate for the Vault server. This certificate includes both the public and private keys. The certificate must be in pfx format.
Because the certificate was not created onthe Vault server, and it includes both the public and private keys, the certificate must be protected so that it doesn't endanger the private key.
-
Transfer the Vault server certificate in *.pfx format and the chain.
-
Back up the current server private key. You can find the key's location in the ServerPrivateKey parameter in the DBParm.ini file.
-
Go to the Vault server installation folder. The default location is C:\Program Files (x86)\PrivateArk\Server).
-
Open the Command window as an Administrator, and run the following command:
CACert.exe import
-
Enter the full path and certificate file name.
-
Restart the Vault application.
View and verify the Vault server certificate
This procedure describes how to view the Vault server certificate.
-
Go to the Vault server configuration folder. The default location is C:\Program Files (x86)\PrivateArk\Server\Conf).
-
Open the DBParm.ini file, and locate the ServerCertificateFile configuration.
-
Go to the folder path location of the ServerCertificateFile.
-
Copy the certificate file into the same folder, and rename the file to the .cer format, for example, Server.cer.
-
Double-click the copy of the file (in the .cer format) to open the file, or use Crypto Shell Extensions.
Verify the Vault server certificate and certificate chain for the TLS connection
-
Go to the Vault server installation folder. The default location is C:\Program Files (x86)\PrivateArk\Server).
-
Open a Command window as an Administrator.
-
Run the verify command:
CACert.exe verify
For more information about the requirements for the Vault certificate, see Prerequisites.

Configure trusted connections between Vault and PTA
You can configure the Vault to send secured syslog data to PTA, and you can configure PTA and the Vault to communicate over TLS.
| 1. | Follow the instructions in Import your Organization's SSL Certificate to create the Server Certificate. |
|
The Vault requires that the SSL Certificate and Certificate Chain are in Base-64 format. |
| 2. | Upload the Server Certificate to the Vault. |
| a. | Run the following OpenSSL command to convert the Root or Intermediate Certificate from a Base-64 Cer file to a PEM file. |
|
| b. | Upload the PEM file to C:\Program Files (x86)\PrivateArk\Server in the Vault machine. |
| 3. | Specify the following parameters in the dbparm.ini configuration file. |
For details on the dbparm.ini configuration file, see DBParm.ini.
- SyslogServerPort=<secure port number>
- SyslogServerProtocol=TLS
- SyslogTrustedCAPath=<PTA certificate PEM file>
| 4. | Save the file and close it. |
| 5. | Restart the Vault. |
| 6. | On the PTA machine, open the local systemparm.properties configuration file using the LOCALPARM command. |
| a. | Press i to edit the file. |
| b. | Value the syslog_inbound parameter as described in systemparm.properties. clientVerification must be set to False, which is the default value. |
The Vault version must be 14.0 or higher and configured to work with TLS. For details, see Configure TLS protocol for the Vault.
-
For TLS 1.3, all Windows-based components must be installed on Windows 2022.
-
After migrating, if you have a previously configured TLS communication from PTA to the Vault, you must copy the configured Vault certificate to the destination PTA server in the same location as it was in the origin server. You must also validate that the file is readable by the OS user casosServices or the OS group pta_server.
-
Specify the following parameters in the Vault.ini configuration file on the PTA server:
Parameter Description ADDRESS Vault address
Must have the same value as the Vault's server certificate extension Subject Alternative Name
VaultCommunicationProtocol Defines the communication type
Valid values: Casos, TLS
For TLS communication, set TLS
TLSVersions
TLS_1_2 or TLS_1_3
TLSPort The port used for TLS communication
Default value: 443
The TLS port must be the same on the Vault server
Required when VaultCommunicationProtocol=TLS
VaultCertificateStore Path that points to a cert bundle that includes the CA certificate or to the CA certificate file itself. This file must be readable by the OS user casosServices or OS group pta_server.
For example, the value for RHEL Cert Bundle is "/etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem".
Use the following path to upload the CA certificate for seamless PTA DR implementation: "/etc/opt/pta/diamond-resources/client-certificates/".
-
Save the file and close it.
-
Restart the PTA application.

PSM for SSH installation
Before you begin
-
Make sure you review the information in PSM for SSH pre-installation tasks.
-
The PSM for SSH installation process preserves the native SSHD on the PSM for SSH machine and interacts with it using dedicated PAM (Pluggable Authentication Module) and NSS (Name Service Switch) modules. This makes the product less invasive and enables each customer to perform the desired configurations and updates according to organizational policies, without making an impact on the PSM for SSH functionality.
Installation
-
On the system console, do the following to install PSM for SSH package (RPM):
Root user rpm –i <CARKpsmp rpm location>/CARKpsmp-<version>.<arch>.rpm
Sudo user sudo rpm –i <CARKpsmp rpm location>/CARKpsmp-<version>.<arch>.rpm
-
On the system console, do the following to install PSM for SSH package (DEB):
Root user dpkg –i <CARKpsmp deb location>/CARKpsmp-<version>.<arch>.deb
Sudo user sudo dpkg –i <CARKpsmp deb location>/CARKpsmp-<version>.<arch>.deb
|
For more information during installation, use the following switches for the rpm command:
-
-v – Displays additional information while installing.
-
-h – Prints hash marks (#) as installation progresses.
The RPM package installation runs automatically and does not require any interactive response from the user. The DEB package prompts the user for pre-configuration parameters in interactive sessions if neither the /var/tmp/psmpparms file nor the debconf cache for carkpsmp package is present on the system.
When the installation is complete, the following message appears:
|
Followed by the instructions for execution of the psmp_setup.sh script.
The psmpsrv service is installed in /usr/lib/systemd/system.
Configure the vault.ini file for installation
-
Copy the /opt/CARKpsmp/doc/examples/vault.ini file.
-
Open the vault.ini file and specify the parameters of the Vault that will be accessed by PSM for SSH.
During installation, the vault.ini file is copied to the PSM for SSH environment and is used by PSM for SSH to access the Vault. For more information, see Vault.ini.
vi vault.ini
-
Value the Address parameter with the Vault IP.
Address=1.1.1.102
-
For high availability implementations and DR, you can specify more than one Vault IP address, separated by commas, as shown in the following example:
Address=1.1.1.102,1.1.1.232
The first Vault IP address that is specified is used when creating the PSM for SSH environment during installation.
When PSM for SSH is running, if it cannot access the first Vault IP address, it automatically tries to access the next Vault IP address transparently, and no human intervention is required.
-
It is possible to use TLS as the communication protocol to the Vault. The Vault must be version 14 or later. For details, see Configure TLS protocol for the Vault.
To enable TLS communication to the Vault, update the following Vault.ini parameters:
Parameter
Description
VaultCommunicationProtocol
TLS
TLSVersions
TLS_1_2
TLSPort
Enter the same value as the TLSPort parameter set on the Vault side, 443 by default.
VaultCertificateStore
Enter the following information:
-
Path to the system certificate store
-
Path to a specific CA certificate
-
Path to any other directory that holds the CA Certificate
-
Create the credentials file for installation
-
Run /opt/CARKpsmp/bin/createcredfile to create a credentials file for the user that will create the Vault environment during the psmp_setup.sh script execution. This file must be called user.cred.
/opt/CARKpsmp/bin/createcredfile user.cred
You will be prompted for the user name and password. You will also be prompted to use the Entropy file.
Rotate the password use in this command.
We recommend that you clean the history by using the
history -c
command.The user credential file must be placed in a folder that is accessible only for the machine or domain administrator who runs the PSM for SSH installation. We recommend that you delete the credential file after completing the registration.
Vault registration and environment configuration
To register the PSM for SSH instance to the Vault and update the necessary configuration files, run the following command, where vault.ini and user.cred are the files created in the previous steps.
/opt/CARKpsmp/bin/psmp_setup.sh --finalize --vault-ini vault.ini --credfile user.cred
If you are upgrading the package and no vault.ini file is supplied to the script, the existing file at /etc/opt/CARKpsmp/vault/vault.ini is automatically chosen.
When the setup script execution is complete, the message should end with:
PSM for SSH service instance registered in Vault and enabled.
All configuration tasks were completed successfully.
After a successful execution, the PSM for SSH services should be automatically enabled.
If you encounter errors, the detailed logs can be found in the /var/opt/CARKpsmp/temp/psmp_setup.log file.
If you want to manually create the PSM for SSH environment in the Vault, use the PSM for SSH registration tool and enable the psmpsrv service. For details, see PSM for SSH registration tool.

Additions and changes made for PSM for SSH
This section describes the additions and changes made for PSM for SSH at the time of installation.
Linux capabilities used by PSM for SSH
PSM for SSH uses the following Linux capabilities:
|
Capability |
Description |
|---|---|
| Name Service Switch (NSS) |
Enables dynamic resolution of system resources such as users and groups. For example, NSS allows local use of domain users. The configuration file is /etc/nsswitch.conf |
| Pluggable Authentication Module (PAM) |
A set of libraries that provide a configurable authentication platform for applications and the underlying operating systems. PAM enables dynamic authentication configuration and supports authentication by external users, such as active directory users, against a local machine. Configuration files are located in /etc/pam.d which houses separate entry files for each authentication entity (SSHD, su, Sudo, etc.) |
Files added
The following files are added to the system:
-
(/usr)/lib64/security/pam_psmp.so - PSM for SSH service privilege access module
-
(/usr)/lib64/libnss_psmp.so.2 - PSM for SSH service NSS module
-
/etc/pam.d/psmp-auth - PSM for SSH service configuration file
The environment in Privilege Cloud
Location
During installation, a new location is created in Privilege Cloud for the PSM for SSH users. This location is created under the Root location and, by default, is called \Applications. By default, PSM for SSH users will be created under this location but they can be created in any of its sublocations, or in any location in the hierarchy.
Safe
During installation, the following Safes are added
All users that are assigned to the Vault Admin group have Vault Admin permissions, are defined as owners of these default safes, and can access them.
| Safe | Description |
|---|---|
|
PSMPConf |
This Safe contains an internal PSM for SSH logic file that is used to parse the connections string received from the end user requesting access to privileged accounts. |
|
PSMPLiveSessions |
This Safe contains data on PSM for SSH live sessions. |
|
PSMPNotifications |
This Safe contains an internal PSM for SSH file used to communicate with other components. |
|
PSMPADBUserProfile |
This Safe contains the configuration files that define customized profiles for provisioned users. |
|
PSMPADBridgeCustom |
A template provisioning script that can be used to customize provisioning scripts is stored in this Safe. All customized scripts for specific device types must be stored in this Safe. |
|
PSMPADBridgeConf |
This Safe contains the main PSM for SSH-ADBridge configuration files used by PSM for SSH. It is configured to clear history every five days. By default, this Safe is called PSMPADBridgeConf. |
Users
During installation, the following users are created in Privilege Cloud for PSM for SSH:
A unique user is created to enable PSM for SSH to authenticate to Privilege Cloud and retrieve passwords. By default, this user is called PSMPApp_<hostname> although it can be changed.
A credentials file is automatically created during installation to enable the PSM for SSH user to access Privilege Cloud transparently. This credentials file includes the host name of the client machine, enabling the PSM for SSH user to access Privilege Cloud from the machine with the specified hostname, and no other machine. This replaces the IP restriction and removes the dependency on the client machine’s IP address.
When the PSM for SSH user is created, it is automatically given the following authorizations in Privilege Cloud:
| ■ | Audit Users |
| ■ | Add Safes |
This user is automatically made an owner of the PSM for SSH configuration safe, although it must be manually made an owner of all Password Safes that it will access to retrieve passwords to the Provider.
In the PSM for SSH configuration safe, by default PVWAConfig, this user has the following authorizations:
-
Use Password/Use accounts
-
Retrieve Files/Retrieve accounts
-
List Files/List accounts
-
Create Files/Add accounts
-
Update Files/Update password value
-
Update File Properties/Update password properties
-
Rename Files/Rename accounts
-
Create/Rename Folder/Create folder
These authorizations will enable the PSM for SSH user to access the main configuration file, as well as store log files in the Safe, if required.
Also, a PSMPGW user is created.

||||||
|
Solution: |
Open the console log, PSMPConsole.log, in the logs folder and identify the relevant errors.
|
Problems while trying to connect with ssh to the PSM for SSH machine after the installation
|
Problem: |
Access with root user to the PSM for SSH machine was denied when trying to connect with SSH. |
|
Solution: |
In order to secure the PSM for SSH server more effectively, after PSM for SSH installation, the root user will not be able to authenticate to this server remotely using a password. You can connect remotely through SSH either with the root user using SSH key authentication or with a different administrative user that is configured in the PSM for SSH as a maintenance user. |
|
Problem: |
SSH connection to the PSM for SSH machine failed with the following error message: No authentication methods enabled, Authentication failed. The /var/log/secure log file shows the following error: Disabled method keyboard-interactive in AuthenticationMethods list publickey,keyboard-interactive. |
|
Solution: |
Set the SSHD ChallengeResponseAuthentication parameter to Yes. If you are in RHEL 9 or later, or if you manually changed the ChallengeResponseAuthentication parameter to No, set it to Yes in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file. Additionally, if the parameter is set in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/50-redhat.conf file, update it there. |
